title: Geometric Universality and Thermodynamic Microstructure of Real Fluids in a Unified Entropic Framework
authors: Carlos E. Romero-Figueroa, Jose Miguel Ladino, Sasha A. Zaldivar, Hernando Quevedo
abstract: We introduce a unified entropic framework for real fluids that encompasses the van der Waals, Berthelot, Redlich Kwong, and Peng Robinson equations of state within a common thermodynamic description. The corresponding microscopic interactions are then explored using Geometrothermodynamics, GTD, through the scalar curvature $mathcal{R}$ of the equilibrium manifold. We show that curvature singularities accurately reproduce macroscopic critical phenomena, while vanishing curvature $\mathcal{R}=0$ identifies specific thermodynamic states where attractive and repulsive intermolecular forces effectively balance. Furthermore, we introduce a set of dimensionless critical-amplitude ratios $Q^i_{j}$, which reveal universal geometric features of the critical regime. Although individual critical amplitudes exhibit a logarithmic dependence on the system size, these invariant ratios organize different molecular species according to the strength of criticality and encode universal scaling features, suggesting their potential as robust classification parameters. Finally, employing Bayesian inference and Markov Chain Monte Carlo, MCMC methods, we statistically reconstruct the zero-curvature curves. The posterior distributions support the consistency of the geometric scaling behavior, demonstrating that the GTD manifold encodes non-trivial information about the underlying thermodynamical models.
summary: This paper unifies several equations of state for real fluids within a novel geometric framework called Geometrothermodynamics (GTD). By analyzing the curvature of the thermodynamic manifold, the authors show that macroscopic phenomena like critical points are encoded geometrically. This provides a powerful, universal tool for classifying and understanding fluid behavior based on fundamental mathematical invariants.
main_problem: To develop a unified entropic framework for real fluids that encompasses multiple existing Equations of State (EoS) within a common thermodynamic description.
main_result: The authors show that the geometric structure, quantified by scalar curvature ($\mathcal{R}$), successfully encodes macroscopic critical phenomena and universal scaling features across different fluid models.
method: The study employs Geometrothermodynamics (GTD), mapping the thermodynamic equilibrium space onto a Riemannian manifold whose geometry is analyzed using concepts like scalar curvature and invariant ratios.
model_or_system: The system under study is real fluids, modeled by various EoS such as van der Waals, Berthelot, Redlich-Kwong, and Peng-Robinson. The analysis extends the framework to examine general thermodynamic systems.
key_observables: Scalar curvature ($\mathcal{R}$), dimensionless critical-amplitude ratios ($Q^i_{j}$), zero-curvature curves, and critical parameters ($V_c, T_c, P_c$).
important_parameters: Intermolecular attraction/repulsion strengths, system size (for scaling analysis), and the generalized thermodynamic potential.
main_assumptions: The model relies on a mean-field approximation for intermolecular potentials and assumes thermodynamic consistency can be captured by geometric invariants.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates P–V isotherms for the van der Waals model, demonstrating the Maxwell equal-area construction for first-order phase transitions.
paper_structure: The paper systematically derives generalized EoS forms, maps them onto a GTD manifold structure, calculates critical parameters using geometric invariants (curvature), and concludes by statistically reconstructing zero-curvature curves using MCMC methods.
why_interesting: While focused on classical fluids, the use of advanced geometric tools like GTD to classify universal scaling behaviors is highly relevant for understanding phase transitions in quantum many-body systems where geometry often dictates critical points.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. (a) P–V isotherms of the vdW model for fixed values of N, a, and b, illustrating the evolution of the EoS with temperature T. (b) Maxwell equal-area construction applied to the oscillatory region of the vdW isotherm, replacing the mechanically unstable branch with the coexistence line corresponding to the first-order phase transition.
Fig. 2. (a) Order parameter as a function of T/Tc for the vdW fluid. (b) Phase diagram in the reduced (P/Pc, T/Tc) plane.

Fig. 3. GTD scalar curvature RII versus reduced volume V/Vc for the vdW model under different isobaric regimes relative to Pc (kB = 1, S0 = 0). Panels (a)–(c) show the effect of a and b at fixed N = 10, while (d)–(f) illustrate the dependence on N for a = b = 15. The curvature is normalized as RII →RIIS3U 2.

Fig. 4. (a) Heat capacity CP of the vdW model as a function of the volume V for P < Pc, P = Pc, and P > Pc, with fixed parameters a = 0.1, b = 0.2, and N = kB = 1. The heat capacity exhibits the same divergence structure as the scalar curvature, with singularities occurring at the corresponding phase transition points.

Fig. 5. Microscopic phase diagrams of the vdW model. Stability and metastability regions are shown, with attractive (A−) and repulsive (R−) interactions determined by the sign of RII. The binodal (blue), spinodal (red), and zero-curvature (black) curves are displayed; the red dot marks the critical point (kB = 1, S0 = 0, a = b = 20, N = 5). Panel (a) labels the phases, while (b) shows isotherms for T ∈[0.8Tc, 1.1Tc].
